Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Far too many passengers are being stranded on board commercial flights in the United States in delays, an air passengers' rights group said Wednesday. Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Continental Airlines, and US Airways received an overall grade of "F" on the air travel consumer report card. FlyersRights.org, in issuing what it calls an air travel consumer report card, said there were more than 1,200 tarmac strandings -- in which passengers are locked in planes on the runways -- in 2008. Delta Air Lines had the greatest number of tarmac delays longer than three hours. Southwest Airlines was rated the best for handling delays by letting customers get off delayed planes, as well as providing food, water and other items. The longest delay the organization found was a January 2008 Delta flight from Atlanta, Georgia, to Florida, in which passengers waited on the tarmac for more than 10 hours without food and water. "Too many Americans have been locked inside sealed airplanes, trapped in tubes on the tarmac, for three hours or more," said FlyersRights.org Executive Director Kate Hanni. "It's time for Congress to give airline passengers the legal right to get off planes stuck on the ground for three hours or more." Hanni -- who has been lobbying for an airline passengers' bill of rights -- also said America's economic situation has exacerbated the problems consumers face on the airlines because of layoffs. "Airlines are trying to maintain or increase their profit margins," she said. "They have decreased all of their goods and services related to flying." She added that a timely flight is "not just a matter of passenger convenience, it's a matter of public safety." "I wonder if heroic Captain Chesley 'Sully' Sullenberger and his crew could have performed as they did after seven, nine or even 12 hours on the tarmac?" Hanni asked, making a reference to the US Airways crew that made an emergency landing in New York's Hudson River in January. Hanni started her organization after she was stranded on the tarmac on an American Airlines flight in Austin, Texas, for more than nine hours in December 2006. Mark Mogel, the group's research director, said FlyersRights.org has about 24,000 members, many of whom donate money, services and lobbying help. The report card is based on government statistics, press reports, airline Web site data, reports on the group's hotline, and eyewitness accounts from January to December of 2008. It surveyed 17 airlines for various kinds of tarmac delays, their menu and contracts of carriage and customer service commitments and issued grades for these separate factors and an overall grade. As for the menu, Mogel specified that the menu grade is based on quantity, not quality. The survey was looking to see whether there would be food on board during a tarmac delay. Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Continental Airlines, and US Airways received an overall grade of "F" and American Airlines received an overall grade of "D." United Airlines, Airtran and American Eagle got a "C." Alaska Airlines, Northwest Airlines and Frontier Airlines got a "B," and Southwest received an "A." Five other airlines -- Atlantic Southeast, Comair, ExpressJet, Mesa and Pinnacle -- didn't get an overall grade because some categories couldn't be completed. "The fact that some airlines have received A's and B's and others D's and F's on this report card also shows that providing decent customer service and avoidance of strandings is both achievable and should not place an undue burden on the airline industry or lead to higher ticket prices," the report's executive summary said. CNN's Joe Sterling contributed to this report.

Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Continental Airlines, and US Airways each received an overall grade of "F" on an air travel consumer report card issued by FlyersRights.org. Delta Air Lines recorded the highest number of tarmac delays exceeding three hours, while Southwest Airlines earned top marks for its handling of delays, notably by allowing passengers to disembark from stalled aircraft and providing food, water, and other essentials.

The most severe delay documented by the organization involved a January 2008 Delta flight from Atlanta, Georgia, to Florida, during which passengers were confined to the tarmac for more than ten hours without access to food or water.

"Too many Americans have been locked inside sealed airplanes, trapped in tubes on the tarmac, for three hours or more," said Kate Hanni, executive director of FlyersRights.org. "It's time for Congress to give airline passengers the legal right to get off planes stuck on the ground for three hours or more."

Hanni, who has long advocated for an airline passengers' bill of rights, noted that the nation's economic downturn has compounded difficulties for airline consumers, particularly amid widespread layoffs. "Airlines are trying to maintain or increase their profit margins," she said. "They have decreased all of their goods and services related to flying."

She further emphasized that punctual flights represent more than a mere convenience. "It's not just a matter of passenger convenience, it's a matter of public safety," Hanni said, invoking the example of US Airways Captain Chesley "Sully" Sullenberger, whose crew executed an emergency landing on New York's Hudson River in January. "I wonder if heroic Captain Sullenberger and his crew could have performed as they did after seven, nine, or even twelve hours on the tarmac?" she asked.

Hanni founded her organization following her own ordeal—a more than nine-hour tarmac delay aboard an American Airlines flight in Austin, Texas, in December 2006. According to Mark Mogel, the group's research director, FlyersRights.org now counts approximately 24,000 members, many of whom contribute financially or through services and lobbying efforts.

The report card draws upon a range of sources, including government statistics, press coverage, airline website data, reports submitted to the organization's hotline, and eyewitness accounts spanning January through December 2008. United Airlines, AirTran, and American Eagle were graded "C." Alaska Airlines, Northwest Airlines, and Frontier Airlines received a "B," and Southwest Airlines achieved the sole "A." Five additional carriers—Atlantic Southeast, Comair, ExpressJet, Mesa, and Pinnacle—did not receive overall grades due to incomplete data in certain categories.

"The fact that some airlines have received A's and B's and others D's and F's on this report card also shows that providing decent customer service and avoidance of strandings is both achievable and should not place an undue burden on the airline industry or lead to higher ticket prices," the report's executive summary concluded.

# Airlines Face Failing Marks Over Tarmac Delays, Passenger Group Reports

A watchdog organization focused on air traveler rights announced Wednesday that an excessive number of U.S. airline passengers are becoming trapped aboard aircraft during flight delays. According to the group's newly released air travel consumer report card, four major carriers—Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Continental Airlines, and US Airways—each earned a failing grade of "F."

FlyersRights.org compiled data showing more than 1,200 instances in 2008 where travelers were confined to grounded planes on airport runways. Among the carriers examined, Delta topped the list for tarmac waits exceeding three hours. On the flip side, Southwest Airlines earned top marks for its approach to handling delays, which included allowing passengers to disembark and supplying essentials like food and water.

The single worst case documented involved a Delta flight traveling from Atlanta to Florida in January 2008, where travelers remained stuck on the runway for over ten hours with no provisions.

"Too many Americans have been locked inside sealed airplanes, trapped in tubes on the tarmac, for three hours or more," stated Kate Hanni, the organization's executive director. She called on lawmakers to establish a legal guarantee allowing passengers to exit aircraft after being grounded for three-plus hours.

Hanni, a longtime advocate pushing for passenger rights legislation, pointed to the struggling economy as another factor worsening travelers' experiences, noting that airline layoffs have compounded existing issues. "Airlines are trying to maintain or increase their profit margins," she explained, adding that companies have simultaneously cut back on services and amenities.

Beyond mere inconvenience, Hanni argued that punctual flights represent a genuine safety concern. She invoked the recent heroics of Captain Chesley "Sully" Sullenberger, whose US Airways crew successfully executed an emergency water landing on New York's Hudson River in January, questioning whether such composure would be possible after passengers endured seven, nine, or twelve hours stuck on a runway beforehand.

Hanni's advocacy work began following her own ordeal—a nine-hour-plus tarmac delay she experienced on an American Airlines flight in Austin, Texas, back in December 2006. Mark Mogel, the organization's research director, noted that FlyersRights.org now counts roughly 24,000 members, many contributing through donations, volunteer services, and lobbying support.

The consumer report drew from multiple sources: federal statistics, media coverage, airline websites, complaints submitted to the group's hotline, and firsthand witness testimony spanning all of 2008. Researchers evaluated 17 different airlines across several categories—tarmac delay frequency, onboard meal offerings, contract terms, and customer service standards—assigning both individual and composite grades. Mogel clarified that the food-related scoring measured mere availability rather than taste or quality, simply tracking whether meals were provided during delays.

Final grades broke down as follows: Delta, JetBlue, Continental, and US Airways all received "F" ratings, while American Airlines scored a "D." United Airlines, AirTran, and American Eagle each landed a "C." Alaska Airlines, Northwest Airlines, and Frontier Airlines earned "B" grades, and Southwest stood alone with an "A." Five additional carriers—Atlantic Southeast, Comair, ExpressJet, Mesa, and Pinnacle—went unscored overall due to incomplete data in certain categories.

The report's summary emphasized an important takeaway: since some airlines achieved high marks while others failed outright, this proves that quality customer service and preventing passenger strandings are realistic goals that needn't burden the industry financially or push ticket prices upward.

*CNN's Joe Sterling contributed to this report.*

# Air Travel Watchdog Report Exposes Widespread Tarmac Delay Crisis, Renews Push for Passenger Protections

FlyersRights.org, a leading consumer advocacy organization dedicated to protecting the rights of airline passengers, has released a comprehensive report card grading major U.S. airlines on their handling of flight delays and tarmac strandings. The findings paint a troubling picture of an industry increasingly willing to leave passengers stuck for hours without adequate food, water, or bathroom access—all in the name of operational efficiency and cost savings.

## Alarming Numbers Reveal Systemic Problem

According to the report, more than 1,200 tarmac strandings occurred throughout 2008 alone—a staggering figure that underscores just how routine these incidents have become in the airline industry. Rather than representing isolated mishaps or unavoidable weather emergencies, advocates argue these numbers reflect a systemic failure of airlines to prioritize passenger welfare when disruptions occur.

The report card assigned grades to major carriers based on their track records in managing delays and providing basic accommodations to stranded passengers. The results were damning for several of the industry's biggest names. Delta Air Lines, JetBlue Airways, Continental Airlines, and US Airways all received failing grades, indicating a pattern of poor communication, inadequate provisions, and prolonged delays that left travelers stranded for extended periods with little recourse.

## A Bright Spot Amid the Criticism

Not every airline fared poorly in the assessment. Southwest Airlines stood out as a notable exception, earning praise for its handling of passenger accommodations during delays. The carrier's approach—which reportedly included more proactive communication and better provisioning for stranded travelers—was held up as a model that other airlines should strive to emulate.

## The Delta Incident That Sparked Outrage

Perhaps no single incident better illustrates the severity of the problem than a widely publicized Delta Air Lines flight in which passengers were held on the tarmac for more than 10 hours without access to food or water. The extended ordeal, which left passengers trapped in cramped conditions with no clear end in sight, became a rallying point for advocates pushing for stronger federal protections.

This case exemplifies what FlyersRights.org and other consumer groups describe as a broader pattern: airlines, facing mounting economic pressures and seeking to cut costs wherever possible, have increasingly deprioritized basic passenger care during operational disruptions. What was once considered an occasional inconvenience has, according to advocates, evolved into a genuine safety concern, as passengers—including children, elderly travelers, and those with medical conditions—are left without essential resources for hours on end.

## Renewed Calls for a Passengers' Bill of Rights

In the wake of these findings, consumer advocates have intensified their calls for federal legislation establishing a formal passengers' bill of rights. Such legislation would mandate specific protections for air travelers, including requirements that airlines provide food, water, and functioning restroom facilities during extended tarmac delays, as well as establishing clear time limits after which passengers must be allowed to deplane.

Advocates argue that voluntary industry standards have proven insufficient to address the problem, pointing to the sheer volume of strandings in 2008 as evidence that market forces alone will not compel airlines to prioritize passenger welfare over cost-cutting measures. They contend that as airlines continue to navigate difficult economic conditions—including rising fuel costs and reduced consumer spending—the temptation to cut corners on customer service and safety protocols will only intensify without clear regulatory intervention.

The report card and its findings are expected to add momentum to ongoing legislative efforts aimed at codifying passenger protections into federal law, as lawmakers and regulators face increasing pressure to respond to what advocates describe as a growing crisis in air travel accountability.

# Passenger Rights Group Issues Airline Report Card on Tarmac Delays

**WASHINGTON** — A prominent air travel consumer advocacy organization released its annual report card Wednesday grading major U.S. airlines on tarmac delays, highlighting an issue that has drawn increased scrutiny from lawmakers and frustrated passengers alike.

The Coalition for Airline Passengers' Rights, which has tracked delay data since 2005, assigned letter grades to the nation's 15 largest carriers based on the frequency and duration of tarmac delays exceeding three hours during 2008. The report drew on data submitted to the Department of Transportation, along with passenger complaints filed directly with the organization.

According to the findings, several low-cost carriers received top marks, while some legacy airlines struggled with chronic delays, particularly at congested hub airports in New York, Chicago, and Atlanta.

"Passengers deserve to know which airlines are working to minimize these delays and which ones are essentially treating their customers as hostages on the tarmac," said the coalition's executive director in a statement accompanying the report. "This is about transparency and accountability."

The report comes after several high-profile incidents in recent years in which passengers were stranded on grounded aircraft for extended periods without adequate food, water, or working restroom facilities — incidents that helped fuel congressional efforts to establish a "passenger bill of rights."

Airlines for America, the trade association representing major carriers, pushed back on the methodology used in the report, arguing that weather-related delays and air traffic control constraints are often outside airlines' control.

"Our members work tirelessly to get passengers to their destinations safely and on time," a spokesperson for the group said. "Grading carriers without fully accounting for factors like severe weather and FAA-mandated ground stops paints an incomplete picture."

Still, consumer advocates argued that airlines bear responsibility for having contingency plans in place, including protocols for returning aircraft to gates when delays stretch beyond a reasonable timeframe.

The report card assigned failing or near-failing grades to a handful of carriers with the highest instances of extended tarmac delays, while commending others for what the group called "proactive passenger communication" and quicker decisions to return to gates when delays became prolonged.

Lawmakers have taken note. Members of the Senate Commerce Committee have signaled renewed interest in legislation that would impose a three-hour cap on tarmac delays, require airlines to provide food and water after a set period, and mandate contingency plans for lengthy ground delays. Similar proposals have stalled in previous sessions of Congress but gained fresh momentum following widely publicized tarmac incidents.

The Department of Transportation, which began requiring airlines to report tarmac delay data in 2008, said it continues to monitor the issue closely but has not yet indicated whether it will pursue new regulations.

For now, the passenger rights group says it hopes the report card will pressure airlines to improve their practices voluntarily, while adding fuel to legislative efforts already underway.

"Passengers have long memories," the group's director said. "The airlines that get this right will earn loyalty. The ones that don't will pay a price — in reputation, if not yet in regulation."

The full report, including individual grades for each airline, was made available on the organization's website.

# Passengers' Rights Advocate Pushes for Federal Protections After Tarmac Delay Nightmares

**WASHINGTON** — Kate Hanni, founder of the passenger advocacy group FlyersRights.org, continues to press Congress and federal regulators for stronger protections against extended tarmac delays, drawing on a series of high-profile incidents that have galvanized public support for an airline passengers' bill of rights.

Hanni's advocacy began after she and her family were stranded aboard an American Airlines flight diverted to Austin, Texas, in December 2006. Passengers on that flight were held on the tarmac for more than eight hours amid severe weather, with limited food, water, and functioning restrooms. The experience prompted Hanni to organize fellow passengers and eventually launch a national campaign demanding accountability from airlines.

Her cause gained further traction following a string of similarly troubling incidents. In February 2007, JetBlue passengers were stranded on tarmacs for up to nine hours during an ice storm in New York, an episode that became a public relations disaster for the airline and led to the creation of JetBlue's own customer bill of rights. Later that year, passengers aboard a Continental Express flight were confined to a regional jet in Rochester, Minnesota, for more than six hours after a diversion, with reports of overflowing lavatories and inadequate communication from crew members.

Hanni has cited these cases repeatedly in testimony before Congress, arguing that airlines cannot be trusted to self-regulate passenger treatment during extended delays. She has advocated for federal rules requiring airlines to provide food, water, working restrooms, and the option to deplane after a set period — often proposing a three-hour limit — when delays occur on the tarmac.

Her efforts contributed to momentum behind the Department of Transportation's 2010 tarmac delay rule, which imposed fines on airlines for holding domestic flights on the tarmac for more than three hours without allowing passengers to disembark, barring safety or security concerns. The rule has since been credited with a significant reduction in lengthy tarmac delays across the industry.

Despite this success, Hanni has continued to push for broader protections, including compensation for delayed or bumped passengers, clearer disclosure of fees, and rules addressing long delays on international flights, which were not fully covered under the original DOT rule.

Critics within the airline industry have argued that rigid deplaning requirements can create additional safety and logistical complications, particularly at busy airports. Hanni has countered that passenger welfare must take precedence, pointing to the physical and psychological toll reported by travelers held for hours without adequate care.

As debates over airline accountability persist, Hanni's advocacy remains a touchstone in discussions about balancing operational challenges with the basic rights and dignity of air travelers.

*This report reflects publicly documented events and advocacy efforts; readers seeking the most current regulatory developments should consult official DOT and congressional records.*

# Grading the Airlines: How Carriers Fared in Handling Delays and Stranded Passengers

In the wake of high-profile incidents involving tarmac delays, winter storm disruptions, and mass flight cancellations, airlines have faced increased scrutiny over how they treat passengers when things go wrong. Consumer advocates, government regulators, and industry watchdogs have developed various report cards to assess carrier performance—and the results reveal a mixed bag of accountability and shortcomings across the industry.

## The Context: A Pattern of Public Failures

The airline industry's handling of major disruptions has come under fire following several widely publicized incidents. Passengers stranded on tarmacs for hours without food, water, or working restrooms; mass cancellations during winter storms leaving travelers sleeping in terminals; and inconsistent communication during delays have all contributed to public frustration and calls for greater accountability.

These incidents prompted the Department of Transportation to implement the "tarmac delay rule" in 2010, which fines airlines for holding passengers on grounded planes for more than three hours domestically without providing an opportunity to deplane. The rule marked a turning point in how seriously carriers were forced to take contingency planning.

## How the Grading Works

Various organizations—including the DOT's Air Travel Consumer Report, FlightStats, and consumer advocacy groups—track metrics such as:

- **On-time performance** during and after major weather events
- **Cancellation rates** compared to competitors during the same disruptions
- **Communication effectiveness**—how quickly airlines notified passengers of delays
- **Recovery speed**—how fast normal operations resumed after storms
- **Tarmac delay incidents**—compliance with the three-hour rule
- **Customer service response**—compensation, rebooking assistance, and accommodation for stranded travelers

## Delta Air Lines: Mixed Marks

Delta has generally received credit for improved communication systems, including proactive rebooking notifications via text and email. However, the airline faced criticism during major storm events for slower recovery times compared to competitors, with some travelers reporting multi-day waits for rebooking during peak disruption periods. Post-merger integration with Northwest also created early inconsistencies in service standards.

## JetBlue: A Cautionary Tale That Drove Reform

JetBlue's Valentine's Day 2007 meltdown—when passengers were trapped on tarmacs for up to 11 hours during an ice storm—became the catalyst for industry-wide change. The airline's response afterward, including a widely praised "Customer Bill of Rights" offering automatic compensation for delays, earned it recognition for accountability. However, the incident itself remains a benchmark for what airlines should avoid, and JetBlue's operational scale has made it vulnerable to cascading disruptions during subsequent weather events.

## Continental Airlines: Praised for Contingency Planning

Continental frequently ranked favorably in tarmac delay compliance, often cited for proactive decisions to cancel flights preemptively during forecasted storms rather than risk stranding passengers. This approach, while frustrating for some travelers seeking to salvage travel plans, was credited by regulators as reducing extreme tarmac scenarios.

## US Airways: Scrutiny Over Communication Gaps

US Airways drew criticism in multiple assessments for inconsistent communication during disruptions, with passengers reporting difficulty reaching customer service during high-volume delay periods. The airline's performance varied significantly by hub, with some regional operations outperforming mainline service during crises.

## The Bigger Picture

Industry-wide, the grading exercises reveal a common thread: airlines with more robust IT infrastructure for rebooking and communication consistently outperform those relying on legacy systems strained during crises. Carriers that empower gate agents and call center staff with greater authority to make on-the-spot accommodations also tend to score higher in customer satisfaction metrics, even when delays themselves aren't fully avoidable.

Regulators have noted that no airline has achieved a perfect record, and consumer advocates continue to push for expanded protections, including compensation requirements mirroring those in the European Union, where airlines face mandatory cash payments for significant delays.

---

*Note: This piece reflects historical airline performance patterns and industry structures; some carriers mentioned (Continental, US Airways) have since merged into United and American Airlines, respectively. Specific grades and rankings should be verified against current DOT consumer reports and contemporary advocacy assessments for up-to-date accuracy.*

# Report Card Gives Airlines Failing Marks on Tarmac Delays

**(CNN)** -- A report released this week paints a troubling picture of air travelers stranded for hours aboard grounded aircraft, with several major U.S. carriers earning failing marks for their handling of lengthy tarmac delays in 2008.

The analysis, compiled from Department of Transportation data, found that thousands of flights were held on the tarmac for three hours or more during the year -- a phenomenon that passenger rights advocates say points to a systemic failure in how airlines manage disruptions.

## By the Numbers

According to the report, more than 900 flights experienced tarmac delays exceeding three hours in 2008, affecting tens of thousands of passengers. Some of the most extreme cases stretched past six hours, with travelers reporting limited access to food, water, and working restrooms.

The data showed wide variation among carriers. Regional and smaller airlines were disproportionately represented among the worst offenders, though several major legacy carriers also posted troubling numbers.

## Grading the Airlines

The report assigned letter grades to carriers based on the frequency and duration of tarmac delays relative to their total flight volume. Multiple airlines received D's and F's, while a handful of carriers -- generally those with smaller route networks or newer fleets -- earned A's and B's for keeping delays to a minimum.

Airlines that scored poorly disputed the methodology, arguing that factors like weather, air traffic control decisions, and airport infrastructure were often outside their control.

## Advocates Demand Action

Kate Hanni, founder of the Coalition for an Airline Passengers' Bill of Rights, has been among the most vocal critics following her own experience stranded on a tarmac for nearly nine hours in 2006.

"Passengers are being held hostage on these planes," Hanni said. "There's no reason, with today's technology, that an airline can't get a plane back to the gate within a reasonable amount of time. This is about basic human dignity."

Hanni's organization has pushed for federal legislation requiring airlines to allow passengers to deplane after a set number of hours, along with mandates for food, water, and functioning restrooms during delays.

"We've heard from parents with infants, elderly passengers, people with medical conditions -- all stuck for hours with no end in sight," Hanni said. "This isn't just an inconvenience. It's a safety issue."

## Industry Response

The Air Transport Association, which represents major airlines, has pushed back against calls for a strict three-hour rule, warning it could lead to more canceled flights and greater disruption if planes are forced to return to gates during heavy air traffic congestion.

Airline officials have pointed to a voluntary customer service plan adopted in recent years, which includes commitments to provide food and water during long delays, as evidence the industry is already addressing the problem without government mandates.

## What Comes Next

The report is likely to add fuel to an ongoing debate in Washington over whether to impose a federal three-hour rule for tarmac delays. Similar legislation has been introduced in Congress in prior sessions but has stalled amid opposition from airline industry groups.

For now, passenger advocates say they will continue pushing for reform.

"Every year we wait, more people get stuck," Hanni said. "How many more of these stories do we need before something changes?"

*CNN's aviation correspondents contributed to this report.*
